The Later Phase of Pallava Temple Construction

Pallava temple architecture includes both monuments carved directly from natural rock and temples constructed from separate stone blocks.

During the reigns of Mahendravarman I and Narasimhavarman I, important rock-cut monuments were created. Large-scale structural stone temple construction became especially prominent under Narasimhavarman II, also called Rajasimha.

These forms should not be understood as an absolute rule in which every rock-cut temple was completed before the first structural temple appeared. Both methods were known during the Pallava period, although the later reign of Rajasimha is particularly associated with major surviving structural temples.

The Shore Temple at Mahabalipuram

The Shore Temple stands close to the Bay of Bengal at Mahabalipuram in Tamil Nadu. It is one of the best-known surviving examples of early South Indian structural temple architecture.

The temple complex is generally dated to the early 8th century CE and is principally associated with Narasimhavarman II, or Rajasimha, whose reign is usually placed around 700–728 CE.

Unlike the Five Rathas, the Shore Temple was constructed using individual stone blocks. Its towers reflect the early Dravida style of South Indian temple architecture.

The Three Shrines of the Shore Temple

An important feature of the Shore Temple complex is that it contains 3 principal shrines.

  • 2 shrines are dedicated to Shiva. One faces east and the other faces west.
  • 1 shrine is dedicated to Vishnu. It contains an image of Vishnu in a reclining position, commonly described as Anantashayana.

The Vishnu shrine is situated between the 2 Shiva shrines. The 2 prominent stepped towers belong to the Shiva shrines, while the central Vishnu shrine has a lower, flat-roofed form.

Three shrines, not three towers

The Shore Temple complex contains 2 Shiva shrines and 1 reclining Vishnu shrine. All 3 shrines do not have identical towers.

Architectural Features

The Shore Temple belongs to the South Indian Dravida architectural tradition. In this style, the principal temple tower, called the vimana, typically rises in a series of stepped levels above the shrine.

The temple complex also contains sculptures of Nandi, the bull associated with Shiva. Rows of Nandi figures are among the recognisable exterior features.

Because the temple stands close to the sea, the salt-laden coastal atmosphere has contributed to the weathering of its stone carvings over the centuries.

Kailasanatha Temple at Kanchipuram

Another important monument associated with Narasimhavarman II, or Rajasimha, is the Kailasanatha Temple at Kanchipuram.

Like the Shore Temple, it is an important early structural stone temple of the Pallava period. It is dedicated to Shiva.

The two temples are associated with the same Pallava ruler but are located at different places:

  • Shore Temple: Mahabalipuram, the coastal port town.
  • Kailasanatha Temple: Kanchipuram, the Pallava capital.

This distinction is especially useful in ruler-monument and place-monument matching questions.

Connecting the Main Facts

The Pallava story can be understood as a connected sequence of political and architectural developments.

Mahendravarman I ruled around 600–630 CE, encouraged early rock-cut temple construction and faced the Chalukya ruler Pulakeshin II. His successor, Narasimhavarman I, ruled around 630–668 CE, became known as Mamalla, captured Vatapi around 642 CE and was associated with the great rock-cut monuments of Mamallapuram. Later, Narasimhavarman II, called Rajasimha, ruled around 700–728 CE and was associated with major structural temples, particularly the Shore Temple at Mahabalipuram and the Kailasanatha Temple at Kanchipuram.

Distinctions for Objective Questions

Several facts concerning the Pallavas are closely related but must not be treated as interchangeable.

  • Kanchipuram and Mahabalipuram: Both were Pallava centres, but Kanchi was the principal capital and Mahabalipuram was a port town.
  • Narasimhavarman I and Narasimhavarman II: Both were important Pallava rulers, but Mamalla and Rajasimha were different rulers.
  • Five Rathas and Shore Temple: Both are Pallava monuments at Mahabalipuram, but the rathas are monolithic while the Shore Temple is structural.
  • Shore Temple and Kailasanatha Temple: Both are associated with Rajasimha, but they stand at Mahabalipuram and Kanchipuram respectively.
  • Chalukya victory and Pallava counterattack: Pulakeshin II defeated Mahendravarman I, while Narasimhavarman I later defeated Pulakeshin II and captured Vatapi.

Prelims focus

  • Shore Temple: Mahabalipuram, Tamil Nadu.
  • Dynasty: Pallava.
  • Principal royal patron: Narasimhavarman II, or Rajasimha.
  • Period: Early 8th century CE.
  • Construction: Structural stone temple, not a monolithic ratha.
  • Principal shrines: 2 dedicated to Shiva and 1 to reclining Vishnu.
  • Trap: The Shore Temple is associated with Narasimhavarman II, whereas the Five Rathas are principally associated with Narasimhavarman I.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 6, Temple Architecture and Sculpture, pp. 81–85; Archaeological Survey of India, Group of Monuments Mahabalipuram (1984), section on the Shore Temple, consulted 18 November 2026; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram, Outstanding Universal Value, section The Temples, consulted 18 November 2026; Ministry of Tourism, Government of India, Incredible India, Kailasanatha Temple, Kanchipuram, consulted 18 November 2026.]
